articles.title: Jake Paul Backs Project to Revive US Titanium Sponge Output
articles.summary: Social media influencer turned professional boxer Jake Paul is backing a Silicon Valley startup that’s planning to revive US production of titanium sponge, a...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Social media influencer turned professional boxer Jake Paul is backing a Silicon Valley startup that's planning to revive US production of titanium sponge, a semi-processed form of a metal used in jet engines and missiles.

American Advanced Materials will use funds from a $12.5 million seed round led by Amity Ventures LLC to grow its team and design a commercial titanium sponge plant. Anti Fund, co-founded by Paul and tech entrepreneur Geoffrey Woo, participated in the round along with venture capital firm Human Capital, AAM said in a statement.

Titanium is a critical mineral used in aerospace and military applications, including aircraft frames and engines as well as satellites, ships and submarines. The metal's high strength relative to its weight, along with its resistance to heat and corrosion, makes it difficult to substitute.

While the US retains significant melting and manufacturing capacity, it didn't produce any titanium sponge – the intermediate product between ore and metal – in 2025. Instead, it imported a record 44,000 tons, mostly from Japan, according to the US Geological Survey. The last major US producer, Titanium Metals Corp.'s Henderson, Nevada, plant was idled in 2020.

"Titanium is critical for anything that flies," AAM co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Alex Liegl said in an interview, adding that the timing was right for a new facility. "You have geopolitically driven supply-chain vacuums, where a new entrant can come in and own a category that was neglected or orphaned by incumbents – titanium sponge being a prime example."

While industrial metals aren't familiar territory for many Silicon Valley investors, AAM has assembled a team including veterans from former titanium sponge producers Timet and ATI Inc., as well as engineers from Tesla Inc., Liegl said.

"Venture capitalists are also seeing a government and an industry that are only now willing to partner with early-stage companies," said the CEO, who previously founded a renewable-energy Bitcoin-mining company and a fintech platform for electric vehicles and home electrification.

AAM is targeting initial annual capacity of about 20,000 tons, with a long-term goal of meeting US demand in full. The company is considering both brownfield and greenfield locations, most likely in a US Gulf Coast state, and hopes to finalize details in six to nine months, Liegl said.

articles.title: Verizon CEO Open to Working With Elon Musk's Starlink, But There’s One Deal He Won’t Touch: ‘No Benefit Whatsoever’
articles.summary: On Monday, Verizon Communications Inc. CEO Dan Schulman sees opportunities to collaborate with satellite providers such as Elon Musk’s Starlink, but says the...
articles.body:
Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below.

On Monday, Verizon Communications Inc. CEO Dan Schulman sees opportunities to collaborate with satellite providers such as Elon Musk's Starlink , but says the wireless carrier has no reason to let Space Exploration Technologies Corp. use its network to compete for mobile customers.

Verizon CEO Sees Potential In Starlink Partnerships

Speaking during Verizon's third-quarter earnings call, Schulman acknowledged that satellite connectivity could complement traditional wireless services, particularly in remote areas with limited cellular coverage.

"I do think there is a role for satellite for sure in remote areas. It's a great service for those customers," he said, adding, "And I do think there are ways that we can work together, either directly or through our JV with satellite providers, to provide a complementary service and a differentiated value proposition."

Schulman reiterated that the company has no plans to offer satellite providers access to its network through mobile virtual network operator (MVNO) agreements.

"I will say, and I'll repeat it again, that there are no backdoors to any of our MVNO agreements and I see absolutely no benefit whatsoever to extending an MVNO deal to any satellite provider," he added.

An MVNO, or mobile virtual network operator, sells wireless services using another carrier's network rather than relying entirely on its own infrastructure.

SpaceX Could Need Billions to Challenge Verizon

During the call, Schulman said Verizon takes SpaceX's ambitions seriously and assumes the company will execute its plans successfully.

He argued that competing directly with established wireless carriers would require SpaceX to build a substantial terrestrial network, including 65,000 to 80,000 macro sites, backhaul infrastructure, radio access equipment and significant spectrum resources.

Schulman estimated that such a buildout could take at least four to six years and cost $300 billion to $500 billion over seven to eight years.

He also dismissed the idea that Verizon must offer Starlink network access to prevent rivals from gaining an advantage.

"There is no benefit to Verizon Communications extending an MVNO deal," Schulman said, adding that the company intends to compete aggressively if SpaceX enters the market. "We will punch back hard when that happens," he said.

articles.title: Billionaire investor Nelson Peltz makes move to buy struggling Wendy's
articles.summary: Longtime Wendy's investor and former chairman Nelson Peltz of Trian Partners has reportedly offered $1.4 billion to buy the struggling fast food giant, accor...
articles.body:
Wendy's ( WEN ) may be cooking up burgers for a billionaire soon.

Longtime Wendy's investor and former chairman Nelson Peltz of Trian Partners has reportedly offered $1.4 billion to buy the struggling fast food giant , according to an SEC filing.

Wendy's shares rose 15% in early trading. The company's market cap was $1.17 billion prior to the deal.

A Wendy's spokesperson didn't return a request for comment. A spokesperson for Trian Partners didn't return a request for comment.

Billionaire Peltz — while familiar with the operations — would essentially be buying a dumpster fire.

After nearly two years of struggles competing with the likes of behemoths McDonald's ( MCD ) and Yum! Brands' ( YUM ) Taco Bell, plus upstarts such as Shake Shack ( SHAK ), Wendy's is on the cusp of a large number of restaurant closures.

"With one of its largest franchisees filing bankruptcy in September (although contested by WEN given prior termination of franchise agreement), we think investors likely expect closures to tick higher than expected, but we admit visibility on our side remains somewhat limited and there could still be a range of outcomes," veteran restaurant analyst Andy Barish warned in a recent note.

"That said," he added, "given our view that there are likely additional franchise operators in the system facing challenges with leveraged balance sheets, higher interest rates and profitability pressures from higher beef, labor & build costs (like many others in QSR), we think it is prudent to moderate our development estimates and bake in more potential closures over the next 6-12 months, as the company works to strengthen its system."

Meritage Hospitality Group, one of Wendy's largest franchise operators, with more than 300 locations, filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in September following severe margin pressures and an escalating dispute with corporate headquarters. The company reportedly initiated plans to shutter at least 41 locations. Reports emerged this week that it could close up to 60.

The high-profile bankruptcy only added grease to the smoldering fire that is the Wendy's restaurant base.

Franchisees had already been closing their locations and heading for the hills.

Buried inside Wendy's brutal second quarter earnings call was a mention that 289 locations closed in the US during the first half of the year.

There are about 5,700 Wendy's in the US, and Barish estimated the Wendy's US store base will be around 5,600 by the end of 2027.

The decision on how many more locations will be closed falls on new CEO Bob Wright, who hasn't hidden his view that Wendy's needs to focus on more profitable locations.

articles.title: Amazon paid $3.5M for 1,000+ trailer moves that never happened — Connecticut man gets 2 years in prison
articles.summary: Ameer Nasir will serve two years in prison and three years of supervised release for the scheme.
articles.body:
A Connecticut man is headed to prison after pleading guilty to defrauding Amazon out of millions of dollars in an elaborate logistics scheme.

Ameer Nasir was sentenced to two years in federal prison , followed by three years of supervised release for the crime, in which he defrauded Amazon out of more than $3.5 million. He remains out on a $300,000 bond and will report to prison on Nov. 12.

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

A single line on your car insurance policy could be inflating your premium by up to 30% — here's what to change

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

Nasir pleaded guilty to wire fraud on March 6 after being arrested on May 8, 2025. The wire fraud charge carries a maximum sentence of 20 years in prison. He has also been ordered to pay restitution to Amazon of $3,547,090.93.

Nasir targeted Amazon Logistics via a service called Amazon Relay , which connects trucking companies to transportation assignments. He registered 23 trucking businesses with the retailer's subsidiary, which organizes the transport of trailers between cities, warehouses and fulfillment centers.

According to the Department of Justice , one of those accounts was created in the name of Nasir's business, Pak Express Transport. The others were created under false names or by fraudulently using the names of other trucking and transportation companies.

From December 2019 through February 2021, officials say Nasir used these accounts to sign up for over 1,000 transportation assignments with Amazon Logistics. He manipulated data in the company's transportation management system to give the impression he had completed trailer movements when he had not, virtually checking trailers in and out of the system. He then submitted fraudulent invoices to Amazon Logistics, which were paid.

Amazon has introduced additional fraud controls to Relay to prevent future incidents. For example, drivers must now verify their identities and trailer telematics keep track of shipments that are in transit.

Trailers included GPS technology when Nasir was running his scheme, but he reportedly evaded it by using a manual override to make it appear he had completed the trailer movements.

articles.title: SK Hynix profit jumps 632%, memory chipmaker sees shortage lasting until 2030
articles.summary: SK Hynix stock jumped after the company posted strong results on Wednesday.
articles.body:
US-listed shares of SK Hynix ( SKHY ) rose more than 9% on Wednesday after the memory maker's record profit and revenue quelled investor worries over the AI trade.

South Korean SK Hynix stock ( 000660.KS ) jumped 10%, while peer Samsung Electronics ( 005930.KS ) gained 9%. US-based Micron ( MU ) also rose 4%.

The South Korea-based company reported a 328% jump in quarterly revenue to roughly $78.7 billion, while operating profit surged 632% to about $62.7 billion, delivering an 80% operating margin. Meanwhile, quarter-over-quarter revenue and operating profit increased by 32% and 38%, respectively.

Growth was driven by surging AI data center demand, higher memory prices, and early shipments of HBM4, which SK Hynix expects to replace HBM3E as its mainstream product.

SK Hynix said more than 50% of its 2027-2028 capacity is already committed under long-term agreements. It reiterated that the AI memory shortage will persist through 2030 as adoption expands beyond cloud providers to enterprises and physical AI applications, including robotics and autonomous driving.

Wall Street remains bullish on memory demand. Now in its 14th quarter, the current chip boom has far outlasted historical cycles, which typically lasted eight to nine quarters.

RBC Capital Markets analyst Srini Pajjuri sees a credible path for the cycle to extend another five quarters.

"Robust AI demand, coupled with a shift toward memory-intensive agentic AI, continues to outpace supply, which is constrained by structural headwinds," Pajjuri wrote on Monday.

SK Hynix said it is returning an additional $45 billion to shareholders, bringing the total buybacks and dividends to an unprecedented $75.2 billion this year.

SK Hynix has been one of this year's highfliers. The company, which operates out of South Korea and trades on the Kospi ( ^KS11 ), listed on the Nasdaq earlier this year.

US-listed shares were trading near their IPO price following bouts of volatility in July and earlier this month. Last week, the company shelved plans for a US listing of its Solidigm flash memory unit after facing opposition from regulators and shareholders.

Ines Ferre is a Senior Business Reporter for Yahoo Finance covering the US stock market, publicly traded companies, and commodities.

articles.title: America's Truckers on the Brink With 221 Bankruptcies This Year
articles.summary: Justin Stoneman has been in the trucking industry for 27 years, operating out of central Michigan’s agricultural heartland. Hauling grain and fertilizer arou...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Justin Stoneman has been in the trucking industry for 27 years, operating out of central Michigan's agricultural heartland. Hauling grain and fertilizer around the Midwest, his 12-odd tractor trailers generated more than $3 million in annual revenue during their best times.

Those days are over. In the past year, Stoneman's business has been squeezed by a range of pressures, from war-fueled spikes in diesel prices to rising insurance costs and onerous debts — all of which have pushed him to the brink. In May, his company, Stoneman Trucking LLC, filed for bankruptcy protection, but he has since lost hope and is shifting to chapter 7, to fully shut down operations.

"I'm so frustrated," Stoneman said. "It's like, what about all this 'Drill, baby, drill'?"

Stoneman isn't alone. At a time when affordability issues are at the center of US voters' concerns heading into next week's midterm elections, America's smaller trucking operators are feeling the pinch. Some 221 trucking companies have filed for bankruptcy so far this year, according to data compiled by Bloomberg, extending a three-year spike at sustained levels not seen in decades.

Around two-thirds of small US carriers — typically operating 20 or fewer tractors, and oftentimes only just one — report that revenue is either flat or down compared with the year-ago period, according to a survey of hundreds of such companies conducted over the past two months by freight-management firm Truckstop and Bloomberg Intelligence. Almost 40% of these operators said that in six months, they expected to be out of trucking or weren't sure where they'd be.

Chip Lane, managing partner at the bankruptcy-focused Lane Law Firm in Texas, said he's seen a "massive uptick" in trucking companies approaching his firm to explore restructuring, sometimes as many as three or four in a week. "They are one of the top businesses that we see over and over and over again."

It's a function in part of the economics of getting in on the ground floor in trucking. Smaller operators typically begin as drivers for larger companies, then foster contacts and a reputation to strike out on their own, said Lane. But many don't have the cash to buy a rig outright and often rely heavily on credit. This makes them more vulnerable than industry leaders like J.B. Hunt Transport Services Inc. to rising costs such as the record diesel prices — even when business is still coming in.

articles.title: Changing your name after marriage or divorce? Why skipping the Social Security office will cost you.
articles.summary: Here's how to update a name change with the Social Security Administration.
articles.body:
Nearly 4 in 10 divorces are between people 50 and older, a rate that has soared in the past decade or so.

There's no clear reason why aging Americans are splitting up, but one possibility is that the prospect of a longer lifespan is pushing them to embrace their bonus years with a sense of freedom.

One step that often slips through the cracks during the messiness of the divorce process is updating your name with the Social Security Administration (SSA) if you legally change it in your divorce decree.

This week, the Social Security Administration sent out a revised how-to sheet about the process.

Divorce after 50 is one of the biggest financial transitions a woman can face, Debra Taylor, a wealth adviser and a certified divorce financial analyst at Carson Wealth in Franklin Lakes, N.J., told Yahoo Finance.

"The Social Security name change is the first domino. The DMV, passport office, and banks need your name to match Social Security's records, and so does Medicare, which many of these women are only a few years away from," she said.

Your Social Security number will not change; only the name linked to it will.

If you're still working, a name mismatch on your W-2 can keep earnings from being credited to your record, Taylor added. "At 55 or 60, every one of those years counts."

Of course, it's not only if you're divorced. If you legally change your name because of a new marriage, you also must notify the SSA to get a replacement Social Security card with your correct legal name.

Here's why: The Department of Motor Vehicles and the US State Department often validate your identity against SSA databases before issuing a new driver's license or passport in your new name. And the IRS checks your name against SSA records. A discrepancy between your tax return and your Social Security number can also delay your tax refunds.

Make sure your final divorce decree or marriage certificate explicitly states your new legal name. Otherwise, you may have to file a separate legal name change petition through your local courthouse.

Once you have that document and an unexpired US photo ID, such as your driver's license or passport, you can fill out an application for a revised Social Security card. You can submit the form and your original certified documents either by mail, online, or in person at your local Social Security office.

It's a hassle to some extent, but changing your name with the SSA is free. So that's good news. A replacement card typically arrives by mail within two weeks.

"Always be sure to check your 'my Social Security' account afterward to confirm your name and earnings record are correct," Taylor added.

articles.title: Natural gas emerges as key AI bottleneck, Anthropic S-1 filing shows
articles.summary: Analysts see power as a key bottleneck for Anthropic.
articles.body:
Access to power has emerged as one of the greatest bottlenecks for the AI build-out, with a particular focus on natural gas, which is cheap and abundant in the US.

Anthropic's S-1 filing proves natural gas is "an AI vertical," Melius Research managing director James West said.

"We know power is a constraint to AI and Anthropic's S-1 filing did nothing to assuage that view," West wrote to clients on Tuesday. "AI compute is a natural gas demand story."

Power-intensive data centers are the backbone of the AI build-out. US electricity demand from data centers is expected to double from 2025 to 2027, per research from Goldman Sachs, after 20 years of roughly stagnant energy grid expansion in the US.

To solve that bottleneck, data center developers have increasingly turned to "behind the meter" power, where a data center develops its own electricity-generation infrastructure or buys capacity from an existing energy provider. Parts crucial to that work, such as natural gas turbines made by GE Vernova ( GEV ), are now subject to years-long backlogs as developers look for power.

Anthropic acknowledges as much in its S-1 filing. In a lengthy section of the frontier lab's risk disclosure, Anthropic said that as data center operators increasingly turn toward natural gas-fired generation — and as regulation slows some of those efforts — "we expect increased competition among users for the same natural gas supply and pipeline capacity in those areas."

Anthropic publicly files IPO prospectus, noting strong revenue growth and massive spending

5 unexpected risk factors Anthropic is worried about

Anthropic is losing $80 billion on paper — and just made money where it counts

That competition, the company wrote, "may adversely affect our ability to contract for firm fuel supply and transportation and to secure the pipeline connections and laterals [to] our facilities," not to mention electricity cost increases driven by a steep supply-and-demand imbalance.

Equipment such as transformers, turbines, generators, substations, and power transmission equipment, Anthropic disclosed, "have been subject to extended delivery timelines, price increases, tariffs and national security requirements, and allocation constraints as demand from data center operators and other large electricity consumers has grown."

Perhaps most crucially, Anthropic wrote, "We may be unable to secure firm gas supply and transportation during the development of a facility, causing a planned site to be delayed or abandoned."

This issue — the possibility that a planned facility may not come to fruition because the developer can't get electricity — was brought into focus by a novel force majeure declaration from data center hyperscaler Oracle ( ORCL ), which was denied a natural gas pipeline permit needed to power its Project Jupiter data center site in New Mexico.

articles.title: Bond yields rise slightly ahead of Fed rates decision
articles.summary: Bond yields ticked up Wednesday morning ahead of the Federal Reserve’s decision on interest rates, with investors expecting the central bank to keep borrowing costs steady. The 10-year U.S. Treasury bond yield was trading at more than 5.02 percent as of midmorning, up by roughly 3 basis points from closing time Tuesday. The note dipped…
articles.body:
Bond yields ticked up Wednesday morning ahead of the Federal Reserve’s decision on interest rates, with investors expecting the central bank to keep borrowing costs steady.

The 10-year U.S. Treasury bond yield was trading at more than 5.02 percent as of midmorning, up by roughly 3 basis points from closing time Tuesday. The note dipped below 5 percent last week for the first time since Sep. 23.

The yield on the 30-year U.S. Treasury bond , meanwhile, was up by about 1.5 basis points from Tuesday. The note was trading at roughly 5.32 percent, after topping 5.33 percent earlier in the morning.

Bond yields spiked throughout the summer and early fall due to mounting government debt and rising oil prices .

Officials on the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) will release its decision on interest rates at 2 p.m. EDT on Wednesday, six weeks after it hiked rates by a quarter point to fight inflation.

Investors expect the FOMC to hold rates steady at a range of 3.75 percent to 4 percent, despite inflation rising from 3.4 percent in August to 3.7 percent in September , according to the consumer price index .

Traders are pricing in a 90.6 percent chance of the central bank holding rates Wednesday, according to the CME FedWatch tool .

“The Federal Reserve has resumed policy tightening,” said Seema Shah, the chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, this week in a statement.

“However, because policymakers are responding primarily to energy driven inflation pressures and currency dynamics rather than a materially overheating economy, this is likely to be a relatively shallow tightening cycle,” she added.

After Wednesday, the FOMC will gather once more this year, in early December. Roughly three-fourths of economists CNBC recently surveyed expect policymakers to hike rates at that meeting.

articles.title: The AI trade is back, and it's sorting software stocks into winners and losers
articles.summary: The chip rebound is sorting software stocks into winners and losers, with October's biggest gainers now falling the hardest.
articles.body:
October was the month investors gave this year's beaten-down software stocks a second chance. Four sessions later, they're taking it back and buying cybersecurity instead.

For most of October, the trade was easy to spot: Sell chips, buy software. Through the Oct. 22 close, the median stock in a 45-stock Yahoo Finance software basket was up about 13% for the month, while the iShares Semiconductor ETF ( SOXX ) had lost about 16%.

Then the trade flipped. Since that close, SOXX has jumped about 7%, and the First Trust Nasdaq Cybersecurity ETF ( CIBR ) has gained about as much, while 26 of the 45 software stocks fell through Tuesday.

The reversal is biggest at the extremes. Palo Alto Networks ( PANW ) and CrowdStrike ( CRWD ) are up about 13% since Oct. 22, and Akamai ( AKAM ) and Cloudflare ( NET ) are up 8% to 9%. Each fell at least 10% earlier in the month.

Going the other way, Fair Isaac ( FICO ) is down about 16%, Cognizant ( CTSH ) about 10%, and Intuit ( INTU ) and HubSpot ( HUBS ) 6% to 8%. Each rallied 28% to 39% before Oct. 22. Adobe ( ADBE ), up about 13% earlier in the month, has lost about 8%.

By Yahoo Finance calculations, the third of the basket that did worst in October through Oct. 22 has gained a median 8% since. The best third has lost a median 5%.

Investors are going back to what worked all year. This week's risers are up a median of more than 40% in 2026. The fallers are still down about 9%.

Donovan Jackson, editor of the Chart Report, flagged the risk on Wednesday morning.

"The risk after a run like this is intra-sector rotation," he wrote. "Over the past few months, software and semis have behaved like two separate trades, with money flowing from one to the other. If money moves back into semis, software will likely take a backseat."

Since the Oct. 22 close, the 20 chip stocks in the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) have added nearly $570 billion in market value, according to Yahoo Finance calculations through Tuesday. The rest of the index lost about $40 billion.

"For now, early trading this week looks more like rotation within AI than a broad return of conviction," Vanda Research's Viraj Patel wrote Wednesday.

Software isn't breaking down. The equal-weight SPDR S&P Software & Services ETF ( XSW ) closed at a record on Monday.

Microsoft ( MSFT ), the biggest software name by market cap, reports after Wednesday's close . If its AI business keeps growing, the list of winners could get longer.

articles.title: Jeep, Ram parent Stellantis stock surges on reaffirmed outlook, cost cuts
articles.summary: Stellantis beat third quarter revenue estimates on Wednesday and reaffirmed its full-year outlook as cost cuts and a refreshed lineup showed signs that CEO A...
articles.body:
Stellantis ( STLA ) beat third quarter revenue estimates on Wednesday and reaffirmed its full-year outlook as cost cuts and a refreshed lineup showed signs that CEO Antonio Filosa's turnaround plan is working.

Filosa said in a statement that the company remains "on track to implement at least 40% of the total 6 billion euros [$6.7 billion] in run-rate efficiencies by the end of this year," and as a result, Stellantis reaffirmed its 2026 guidance, with the expectation of positive industrial free cash flow in 2027.

Stellantis's full-year guidance calls for mid-single-digit revenue growth, a low-single-digit adjusted operating margin, and improved industrial free cash flow. Analysts see a 1.65% full-year margin and negative industrial free cash flow of 2.98 billion euros ($3.3 billion). Interestingly, Stellantis has already burned 4.9 billion euros ($5.5 billion) through September, so that estimate implies a fourth quarter inflow of nearly 2 billion euros ($2.1 billion).

Stellantis stock surged 15% in midday trade in New York, but the stock is down 57% year to date.

As for the quarter, revenue rose 1% to 37.6 billion euros ($41.8billion) vs. 36.37 billion euros ($40.5 billion) expected, per Bloomberg consensus. Adjusted operating income climbed to 256 million euros ($285 million) from 90 million euros ($100 million) a year earlier.

Industrial free cash flow came in at a loss of 4 billion euros ($4.5 billion) versus a loss of 3.4 billion euros ($3.8 billion) expected by analysts.

Across regions, North America swung to a 64 million euro ($71 million) profit, helped by the Jeep Cherokee hybrid and the Ram 1500 Hemi V8 .

Europe weighed on results. Stellantis posted a 311 million euro ($346 million) adjusted operating loss there as prices fell and sales shifted toward less-profitable EVs, while BYD, Volkswagen, and Renault added to pricing pressure.

Global shipments, which Stellantis reported earlier this month, slipped 1% to 1.29 million vehicles, just shy of the expected 1.3 million. North America fell 12% to 357,000 versus the 362,500 expected, as planned production downtime hit the Jeep Grand Cherokee and Compass. Enlarged Europe rose 10% to 588,000, ahead of the 578,500 estimate, driven by growth in EV and Leapmotor.

The shutdowns were aimed at clearing US dealer lots. Inventory stood at 368,000 vehicles at the end of September, or 84 days of supply, down from 92 days in June. Stellantis expects that to fall to 320,000-350,000 units by year-end.

Stellantis plans to spend 60 billion euros ($66.8 billion) through 2030 on dozens of new models, prioritizing Jeep, Ram, Peugeot, and Fiat.

articles.body: Bengaluru: Info Edge founder Sanjeev Bikhchandani is set to return to an expanded executive leadership role, taking over as managing director and group CEO from Hitesh Oberoi, who is stepping down after nearly 27 years with the company, including more than 16 years as its MD and CEO.The company’s board has approved Bikhchandani’s appointment as executive vice-chairman, MD and group CEO from Dec 3, subject to shareholder approval. Info Edge has been a defining part of my life, and I feel enormous gratitude and pride when I look back at what we have built together,” he wrote.Oberoi said he was comfortable stepping back after seeing through key priorities across the company’s businesses. Naukri had developed a clear AI and data strategy, 99acres had established market leadership and become a cash-generating business, Jeevansathi and Aisle were profitable, and Job Hai had built a monetisation engine.“More importantly, together, we have built a much stronger institution,” he wrote, pointing to senior leaders with more than two decades at Info Edge and a younger generation ready to take on greater responsibility.“On a personal level, I would also like to spend more time with my family and support some initiatives I have been involved in,” Oberoi said during the analyst call, adding that the company was institutionally stronger and that he felt it was the right time to step back.During his 16 years as CEO, Info Edge’s market capitalisation grew from about Rs 2,500 crore to around Rs 80,000 crore, according to the company. Its portfolio includes recruitment platform Naukri, property portal 99acres, matrimonial platforms Jeevansathi and Aisle, education portal Shiksha and jobs platform Job Hai.Bikhchandani’s appointment is for a term until April 26, 2031, subject to shareholder approval. In a statement, he described Oberoi as an “extraordinary partner” and praised his leadership and judgement.“I shall dearly miss Hitesh — a comrade in arms, a torchbearer for the Company and the Internet industry, a close friend and colleague, an exceptional business leader,” Bikhchandani said, adding that Oberoi would remain available to advise business managers and that he would rely on his guidance.Asked whether he would serve as a full-time CEO or whether the move was part of a broader management transition, Bikhchandani said the leadership structure was yet to be decided. “I will be taking over, listening a lot, observing, asking questions and learning. articles.title: US consumers look resilient despite higher prices for gas, Halloween candy, and more
articles.summary: The US consumer is not crumbling, which is remarkable.
articles.body:
There's an old adage in investing that goes something like this: Don't bet against the US consumer's propensity to spend.

After all the excitement over the Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) IPO prospectus dropping this week, I think the Federal Reserve decision today will bring some focus back to the state of the economy and, by extension, some focus on how the US consumer is faring amid higher prices for gas, Halloween candy , medical expenses, and winter clothing, among other inflationary categories.

I would sum up what I am seeing from consumers right now as remarkable resilience.

Coca-Cola ( KO ) has pushed through commodity-based price increases , yet Coke Zero sales increased 16% in the third quarter. Though new Coke CEO Henrique Braun did sound a touch measured about the consumer in an interview on Yahoo Finance.

It's not getting any cheaper to stay at a Hilton ( HLT ) property, yet its third quarter earnings release this week showed strong spending on rooms .

Delta ( DAL ) said earlier this month that it's continuing to see strength in premium seats and upgrades.

Visa ( V ) said last night that fiscal fourth quarter sales rose 13% from the prior year. Initial guidance for fiscal year 2027 highlighted the potential for double-digit sales growth.

"Growth across consumer spend bands remained relatively consistent with prior quarters, with the highest spend band continuing to grow the fastest. We did not see signs of the lower-spend consumer weakening in our volumes," Visa CFO Chris Suh said on the earnings call.

SoFi ( SOFI ) blew investors away with its third quarter results , fourth quarter outlook, and first crack at 2027 guidance. It feels so confident in its business that it also released bullish 2030 guidance.

This quarter "says that the consumer is very strong," SoFi CEO Anthony Noto told Yahoo Finance . "We saw strong demand for our products. Our credit performance was very solid. The spending that we saw in SoFi money and debit spending was very strong as well as credit spending. We saw good inflows in the investment business where people are looking to put money to work to help them accomplish their objectives. So I would say the consumer has been very stable and strong."

If you are looking for reasons for the surprisingly strong upside moves in Target ( TGT ) and Macy's ( M ) stock in recent months, this consumer resilience is why. Even Walmart's ( WMT ) stock has come alive and is up 11% in a month.

Maybe think twice about betting against the US consumer this holiday season.

articles.title: From Texas to Ohio, the data center backlash is spilling over into the midterms
articles.summary: With the midterm elections just a week away, candidates are seizing on the backlash to data centers.
articles.body:
A groundswell of opposition to data center development in communities across the country has increasingly real consequences for the future of artificial intelligence and the upcoming midterm elections.

Data center companies pitch the projects as economic development that will boost the local tax base, Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution's Center for Technology Innovation, told Yahoo Finance. And there was a time when communities would pay incentives to attract that development.

"But people are not buying this argument anymore," West said. "In fact, they actually want companies to start paying their community for the right to build the data center in that area."

Now, with the midterm elections just a week away, candidates are seizing on that backlash and wielding the issue as a weapon against opponents. It's particularly fraught in Texas and Ohio, states with lots of data centers and tight Senate races.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott is running against James Talarico, a Democratic state lawmaker. West noted, "Governor Abbott a year ago was very supportive of data centers."

Since then, he has halted new permits for data centers while the state conducts energy and water audits.

In Ohio, Democrat Sherrod Brown, who is seeking a return to the US Senate, has called his GOP opponent Jon Husted "the face of data centers" over Husted's previous support for giving tax breaks to data centers.

The data center construction boom, meanwhile, is shifting from blue states to red states. Democratic strategist Steve Rattner recently posted on X that while 56% of currently operating data centers are located in blue states, 66% of planned data centers are in red states.

Excluding Virginia, the nation's leader in data center capacity, 92% of the planned build-out is in red states, Rattner noted.

The opposition among voters, however, is more bipartisan.

"Both Republicans and Democrats are worried about data centers," West said.

Molly Moorhead is economics editor for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title: Your bank isn’t supposed to judge your beliefs. The administration just proved some did.
articles.summary: An extensive report by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency has confirmed that major U.S. banks engaged in widespread politicized debanking of individuals and businesses due to their religious, social, or political views.
articles.body:
For years, Americans who lost their bank accounts over their beliefs were told they were imagining things. Banks sent form letters. Customer service read from scripts. Nobody would say why. The federal regulator that oversees the nation’s largest banks recently confirmed what many of us have argued all along: politicized debanking was real, it was widespread, and it can easily happen again.

President Trump issued an executive order in 2025 to address politicized debanking. To carry it out, the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency spent months examining the nine largest national banks it oversees. The OCC reviewed nearly 100,000 complaints, hundreds of individual bank decisions, and about 420,000 pages of internal bank documents. The result is an extensive report called “ Debanked: Guaranteeing Fair Banking for All Americans .” It found that these banks used broad “reputation risk” policies, with no clear standards and no objective, risk-based criteria, to “disadvantage” Americans because of their political, religious and social views. Debanking also hit businesses that offended the progressive sensibilities of bank employees, like those in the oil and gas, coal, and firearms industries.

As an attorney, I read a lot of corporate policies. Most are dull. These were troubling. One bank told employees to scrutinize “controversial clients,” and it listed “religious leaders” among them. Banks treated the opinions of “advocacy groups,” “activist groups,” and “elected officials” as factors in deciding whom to serve. Some relied on the Southern Poverty Law Center, a hyper-partisan and deeply discredited group, to flag customers for cancellation. As if that weren’t enough, the SPLC itself now faces criminal indictment on charges that include money laundering and making false statements to a federally insured bank.

A JPMorgan-owned payment processor closed the account of an organization described as a “[r]ight wing religious conservative non profit,” and a bank employee later scrubbed the words “right wing” and “religious” from the records. The same processor shut down an account raising money for a devout Christian’s legal challenge to an anti-discrimination law. PNC turned down a growing media company for a line of credit after an employee wrote that its owners held opinions “very contrary to PNC’s beliefs/values.” TD flagged a faith-based healthcare sharing ministry because its religious requirements appeared to “conflict with TD’s values of diversity and inclusion.”

That should worry everyone, whether or not you share the views or faith of those being targeted today. A bank that can cut off your neighbor for his views can cut you off for yours.

For-profit businesses suffered too, and small businesses are especially vulnerable. Big companies can weather storms. But for a small business, losing the ability to make payroll or pay bills for even a few weeks can be ruinous. The bank practices identified in the OCC report don’t reduce risk. They protect large incumbents and push out smaller competitors.

Many debanked customers never learned the real reason. The report found that closure letters often just cited the bank’s right to close an account “for any reason and at any time.” My colleagues and I have seen this firsthand. In 2023, Bank of America closed the accounts of Indigenous Advance , a Memphis-based Christian charity that serves orphaned and vulnerable children in Uganda, along with a local church that supports it. The bank’s letters used the same boilerplate language the OCC flagged: that the ministry was “operating in a business type we have chosen not to service” and no longer “aligns with the bank’s risk tolerance.”

The report’s most important warning concerns the future. Banks have revised their policies, but some have simply relabeled reputation risk as “franchise” or “brand” risk. The OCC says it cannot say with confidence that current policies will keep banks from returning to these practices, and no bank has fully and publicly acknowledged its past debanking decisions. Trump’s executive order declared that no American should be denied financial services because of protected beliefs, affiliations or political views, and it set this OCC report in motion. But executive orders and regulators change with administrations. Laws passed by legislatures provide durable protection.

That’s why the states matter. Tennessee, Idaho and South Carolina have passed legislation to protect consumers from discriminatory debanking. These bills were based on Alliance Defending Freedom models. The report found that state laws like these likely pushed many banks to rethink their industry-based restrictions. Other states should follow their lead. They should require banks to give customers specific reasons when they are cut off, prohibit decisions based on protected speech, religious exercise, or engagement in a lawful business, and give harmed Americans a real legal remedy.

Large banks benefit from wide-ranging government support, including greater lending power, FDIC insurance rates, subsidies, bailouts, and an anticompetitive chartering system. In return, they owe every American fair treatment. Your bank account should depend on measurable financial risk, not on your faith or your politics.

Jeremy Tedesco is senior counsel and senior vice president, global censorship at Alliance Defending Freedom ( @ADFLegal ).

articles.title: Brewers' World Series run may give Wall Street a reason to root for Milwaukee
articles.summary: The Milwaukee Brewers are one win from their first World Series title, and history says the stock market tends to do a bit better after a National League tea...
articles.body:
The Milwaukee Brewers are one win from their first World Series title, more than five decades after starting out as the bankrupt Seattle Pilots. The stock market has its own reasons to cheer them on against the Tampa Bay Rays.

The stock market has risen in about 71% of the years after a National League team won the World Series, compared with 67% for all years since 1928, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. A Rays comeback would mean an American League title won in seven games, and the market has risen after only six of those 14.

Think of it as the market's batting average. The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) has hit .714 in the year after a National League title and .636 after an American League win, against a lifetime mark of .673. Average gains line up the same way, about 11% after NL wins, about 8% for all years, and about 6% after AL wins.

Stocks rise in most years, regardless of who wins. Read strictly, the idea that an NL title means stocks go up and an AL title means they go down has been right 50 times in 97 World Series. That's a coin flip.

The seven-game AL record also comes with an asterisk. Seven of the eight down years that followed one came between 1945 and 1973, and stocks rose after four of the five since 1985.

Milwaukee's World Series history comes with good market timing

The city's baseball history has a curious habit of showing up near stock market lows. The Milwaukee Braves won the 1957 World Series on Oct. 10, and the bear market hit bottom 12 days later. The S&P 500 then gained 38% in 1958.

The Brewers' only other series trip, in October 1982, came two months after the low that started the long bull market of the 1980s and 1990s. They lost to the St. Louis Cardinals in seven games.

The Rays haven't been as lucky with their timing. Their first World Series, in 2008, came during the S&P 500's worst month since 1987. Their second came in 2020, the pandemic year.

None of this means a baseball game moves stock prices. Either way, a first-time champion is guaranteed, and the market rose in the year after 10 of the 13 first titles since 1935.

Game 5 starts at 8 p.m. ET Wednesday in St. Petersburg, Fla. A Brewers win ends the series. A Rays win sends it back to Milwaukee for Game 6 on Friday and keeps the seven-game scenario alive.

articles.title: India’s robotics market may quadruple by 2030
articles.summary: India’s robotics market may top $4.6B by 2030, driven by warehouse automation; imports still dominate components, while Indian integrators eye global growth.
articles.body: BENGALURU: India’s robotics market could more than quadruple to $4.6 billion by 2030 from $1.1 billion in 2025, helped by growing demand for warehouse automation from e-commerce and quick commerce, according to Avendus Capital.The expansion, however, rests heavily on foreign hardware. Imports account for 85-90% of robotic component value, including sensors, motors and precision parts, the investment bank’s report said.Avendus identified warehouse and logistics automation as India’s strongest robotics opportunity. Domestic companies are building systems that combine machines with software to move, store and sort goods, with Indian platforms already being deployed overseas.Rising wages are also making automation easier to justify. Payback periods for lower-cost automation have shortened to about 1.5-2 years, compared with several years a decade ago, the report added.India’s opportunity lies in integrating these systems into customers’ operations and deploying them repeatedly across locations. That gives companies scope to build businesses even as a domestic component ecosystem develops.Replacing imported hardware will take longer. Precision components require manufacturing consistency, reliability and lengthy customer approvals, capabilities that established Japanese and German suppliers have built over decades. Avendus expects localisation to proceed component by component.The next commercial test for Indian warehouse automation companies is winning repeat contracts across multiple overseas sites. Those orders would demonstrate that businesses can expand beyond individual projects and turn their early deployments into recurring demand, the report said.You use AI every day.
